records.name_note: The currently accepted binomial is Lilium longiflorum — used consistently by NC State Extension, Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden, and confirmed by RHS's own "Name Status: Correct" tag. NC State notes the species was previously classified under two infraspecific names, Lilium longiflorum var. eximium and Lilium longiflorum var. nobile. One admissible source conflicts: Penn State Extension's "Easter Lily, a Herald of Spring" names the plant "Lilium wallichianum, formerly Lilium longiflorum" in its opening line and photo caption. This is inconsistent with the other four sources (including Penn State's own separate "Spring Holiday Plants and Pets" article, which uses Lilium longiflorum) and with RHS's explicit "Correct" status for Lilium longiflorum, so Lilium longiflorum was retained as scientific_name_accepted with this conflict documented rather than silently resolved.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a damage-onset cold temperature for L. longiflorum specifically — only survival-oriented hardiness data exists (NC State zones 5a-8b; Missouri Botanical Garden zone 4-8; RHS Hardiness H3, -5 to 1°C / 23-34°F; Penn State 'hardy to USDA zones 4 through 8'), which per the task's own guidance should not be mapped onto a damage-onset field.

night_f_min / night_f_max: Clemson ('slightly cooler night temperatures') and Penn State ('slightly lower temperatures at night') both note nights should be cooler than the 60-65°F daytime range, but neither gives an exact number.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good / direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives footcandle figures or a specific outdoor sun-hour ceiling for this species; sources only give the categorical 'full sun' / 'part shade' terms.

humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: Clemson and Penn State both instruct avoiding dry air from heating ducts, fireplaces, or appliances, but neither source gives a percentage or explicitly labels a humidity category (low/average/high).

soil_base: garden culture is described as 'well-drained soil enriched with organic matter' (Clemson, RHS, Penn State); for containers RHS separately specifies 'peat-free, loam-based potting compost...with added grit and leaf mould.' Neither description maps cleanly onto a single schema soil_base category.

water_regime: genuine cross-source conflict, left null. Missouri Botanical Garden ('Bulbs need good moisture year-round. Do not allow soil to dry out.'), NC State ('Mulch and maintain even moisture'), and Penn State ('They prefer even moisture...Never allow the plant to sit in standing water') all describe keeping soil continuously moist, while Clemson instructs 'Water the plant thoroughly when the soil surface feels dry, but avoid overwatering' -- a let-the-surface-dry-then-water approach.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: Clemson gives only qualitative fertilizing guidance ('a complete fast-release fertilizer such as 8-8-8...when the new shoots emerge and monthly until flowering,' or a single spring application of slow-release fertilizer) with no explicit day-interval number, calendar months, or dilution/strength figure.

water_check_depth_cm / water_dry_down_target / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives numeric watering-interval, check-depth, or dormancy-duration estimates for this species.

soil_ph is well supported (Clemson 6.5-7.0) but note RHS separately describes the species more broadly as tolerant of 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' soil -- not a numeric conflict, but the broader RHS tolerance statement was not used to override Clemson's specific target range.

cool_rest_note — removed on audit: The six-week chilling-requirement claim traces to exactly one citation: Penn State's 'Easter Lily, a Herald of Spring.' I fetched that page directly and its body text repeatedly names the plant 'Lilium wallichianum' (not just in the photo caption already quoted in name_note, but in the descriptive sentence 'The Easter lily (Lilium wallichianum) is a member of the Liliaceae family'). The record's own name_note already distrusts this exact article's species identification enough to exclude it from scientific_name_accepted -- yet the same conflicted article is the sole support for a specific numeric horticultural claim (six weeks) with no independent corroboration. I checked both Clemson's and NC State's full Easter Lily pages directly for any chilling/vernalization language and found none on either page. A number resting solely on a source the record itself flags as unreliable for basic species ID, with zero cross-source corroboration, should not have been accepted as confidently as a plain unknowns-free field.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Minor traceability gap: toxicity_detail states cats 'may also show disorientation, staggering, and seizures.' I fetched the Clemson page and confirmed this sentence does appear there verbatim ('They may also experience disorientation, staggering, and seizures') -- so the underlying fact is accurate -- but the citation entry's own quote field is truncated and stops at '...will occur within 6 to 12 hours of ingestion,' omitting that clause entirely. Per the structural check ('does every non-null field value trace to at least one entry in citations'), this clause of the field's prose is not actually present in any citation's quote text, even though the source itself supports it. This is a citation-completeness defect, not a factual error.

records.name_note: scientific_name_accepted is left null on a genuine, unresolved naming conflict between two admissible sources. RHS's Rhododendron simsii species page lists its synonym as "Azalea indica Sims" (the 1817 epithet). NC State Extension independently maintains a live page for a different currently-accepted species, Rhododendron indicum ("Southern Indian Azalea"), stating "Previously known as: Azalea indica" -- the bare, unauthored 1753 Linnaean epithet. Both historical "Azalea indica" names are in play, and they resolve to two different modern binomials; without knowing which lineage a given nursery specimen traces to, this catalog cannot safely assert Rhododendron simsii as the accepted name from RHS's page alone. Toxicity below is sourced at the genus/common-name ("azalea"/"Rhododendron spp.") level, which both historical lines share, so the naming gap does not weaken it.
records.toxicity_detail: Two independent US extension sources, both naming azalea specifically (not just the Rhododendron genus in the abstract), corroborate pet toxicity with more than boilerplate detail. UGA Cooperative Extension's dedicated pet-safety circular gives "Rhododendron Azalea" its own entry classed "Major Toxicity" ("May result in serious illness or death if ingested"). UF/IFAS's poisonous-landscape-plants publication explains the mechanism for its "Azaleas (Rhododendron and Azalea spp.)" entry: grayanotoxin glycosides present in all parts of the plant (including flowers and nectar) disrupt sodium channels, producing neurologic, gastrointestinal, and cardiovascular dysfunction, with poisoned animals initially showing anorexia, excessive salivation, vomiting, and frequent defecation.
records.cool_rest_note: After flowering, give the plant a cool, moist rest: RHS recommends siting it in a cool, moist area of the greenhouse with night temperatures around 45-50°F (7-10°C).
unknowns: chill_damage_f: the RHS Indoor Azaleas guide notes frost sensitivity ('bring under cover... before any risk of frost') but gives no specific damage-onset temperature in °F; the species page's H4 hardiness rating (-10 to -5°C) is a survival/hardiness class, not a damage-onset figure, so left null.

day_f_min/day_f_max and general night_f_min/night_f_max: RHS gives ambient greenhouse temperature ranges (55-61°F normal; 65-70°F for forced reflowering) without splitting day vs. night; only a rest-period-specific night temperature (45-50°F) was found, and that is captured in cool_rest_note rather than as a general night range.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: the species-specific RHS source gives only a categorical 'Acid' pH with no numeric range; general (non-species-specific) azalea Extension pages disagree on numeric range (Clemson 4.5-6.0 vs. UMD 4.5-5.5), so left null rather than pick a side.
humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source gives a numeric relative-humidity percentage for this species.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: sources give only a position/duration category (partial shade), never a footcandle or sun-hour figure.

water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: no source gives a watering interval in days or a moisture check-depth for this species; only the qualitative rule 'never let the compost dry out' was found.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months: RHS specifies feeding 'on two or three occasions up until the end of June' beginning 'when the first signs of new growth are seen,' without a numeric day interval or a named start month, so left null.

humidity_need — removed on audit: Set to 'high' but direct verification of the RHS 'Azaleas Indoors' page shows the word 'high' (or any graded humidity level) never appears -- only the unquantified term 'humid'/'cool, humid atmosphere'. Additionally the citation's claim label reads 'cool, humid atmosphere with daily misting,' but 'daily misting' is not in the quoted sentence at all -- it's pulled from a different, uncited sentence in the watering section ('Mist daily and water as needed'), inflating support for the categorical jump to 'high'.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: Categorized as 'moisture_retentive,' but the verbatim RHS field value is the combined phrase 'Moist but well-drained.' The chosen category foregrounds moisture retention and drops the explicit well-drained/free-drainage requirement paired with it in the source, which risks misleading care guidance (encouraging water-holding rather than free-draining acidic mix).

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: the first pass's only citation was a truncated, boilerplate-flavored RHS pet-safety tag with no species-specific detail. A second research pass, prompted specifically to find independent corroboration, found UGA and UF/IFAS entries naming azalea/Rhododendron spp. with a documented toxin mechanism (grayanotoxin) -- both now cited above.
scientific_name_accepted: left null after the second pass surfaced a real cross-source naming conflict (see name_note) rather than the simple absence-of-evidence the first pass's null reflected.

citations.claim: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail — grayanotoxin mechanism, UF/IFAS poisonous landscape plants publication
citations.source: University of Florida IFAS Extension, ENH1384/EP648, "Common Poisonous Landscape Plant Species in Florida"
citations.quote: many landscape plants can be toxic if consumed, posing risks to small children, pets, and livestock such as cattle, horses, or sheep ... Azaleas (Rhododendron and Azalea spp.) ... unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max and night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives target day/night temperature ranges for this landscape shrub.
humidity_need and humidity_pct_min/max: not addressed by any admissible source (outdoor landscape/garden extension sources don't discuss ambient humidity for this species).

light_fc_min/light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max: admissible sources give sun-duration categories (full sun / part shade) rather than footcandle values or an hours-of-sun ceiling, so per field notes these were left null rather than forced.

soil_base: no admissible source categorizes the growing medium with a substrate label (e.g. standard potting mix, cactus mix); sources only describe in-ground soil texture and pH tolerance for a landscape shrub.

soil_drainage (fast/moderate/moisture_retentive): Clemson ('must have good drainage...will not do well in wet areas'), RHS ('moist but well-drained'), and UF/IFAS ('well-drained') all require good drainage but none uses a fast/moderate/moisture_retentive category label, so this was left null rather than guessed.

water_regime and the water_* estimate fields: sources describe general drought tolerance once established (Clemson: 'very drought-tolerant... respond well to occasional deep watering'; UF/IFAS: 'very drought tolerant, but moist soils or irrigation stimulate growth') but none frame watering as a moisture-check cycle matching the schema's regime categories, so this was left null rather than force-fit.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: UF/IFAS (ST418, a cultivar-specific fact sheet whose Culture-section statements are framed as applying to oleander generally) states it grows 'well with only one yearly fertilization and springtime pruning,' and UF/IFAS EP574 separately notes 'established plants usually do not need fertilizer' — but neither gives an explicit day-interval number or calendar month, so these numeric fields were left null.
cool_rest_note: not addressed by any admissible source.

chill_damage_f: used NC State's damage-onset figure (32°F, 'intolerant of temperatures at or below 32 degrees F...may be damaged'). Clemson separately states oleander 'will survive temperatures down to 15 to 20 °F, although their foliage will be damaged' — a survival floor, not a damage-onset figure — so that number was not used for this field to avoid conflating onset with survival.

toxicity_detail intentionally omits the extended human poisoning symptom list (nausea, vomiting, irregular heartbeat, dilated pupils, bloody diarrhea, etc.) that NC State lists under a general 'Poison Symptoms' field with no explicit pets-only counterpart, to avoid presenting human-specific symptom detail as verified for pets; toxic_to_pets itself is instead supported directly by NC State's dedicated 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' flags and RHS's explicit 'TOXIC to pets if eaten' statement.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The sentence 'Sap contact can cause skin irritation/contact dermatitis' has no supporting citation anywhere in the citations array. Citation #5 (Clemson) is labeled 'toxicity_detail smoke from burning is toxic' and its quote text is only 'Smoke from burning cuttings can cause severe reactions.' — it does not contain the sap/skin-irritation claim. I fetched the live Clemson page and confirmed it does say 'Contact of sap with skin may cause irritation,' and the live NC State page has a separate structured field 'Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes' — both would support the claim, but neither was captured as its own citation entry with its own quote. As written, this clause in toxicity_detail fails the basic 'every non-null field value traces to a citation' check: the record asserts a specific harm mechanism (contact dermatitis) that no cited quote actually states.

soil_ph_max — removed on audit: The cited UF/IFAS quote is 'It is adaptable to a pH range of 5.0 to more than 8.3.' The source explicitly flags the upper bound as open-ended ('more than 8.3'), not a ceiling — meaning the plant's demonstrated/tolerated upper pH is higher than 8.3, with the true max unstated. The record nonetheless encodes soil_ph_max as the flat number 8.3, converting the source's explicit 'more than' qualifier into a hard cap. This re-derives a number that is only a floor-of-the-unknown-upper-range in the source, not the actual maximum, understating what the source itself says about pH tolerance.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note states 'All admissible sources consulted (NC State, Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, RHS) use "Nerium oleander" as the current accepted name.' But no citation in the citations array is from Missouri Botanical Garden (no plantfinder.mobot.org or www.missouribotanicalgarden.org URL appears anywhere in the record). This is a direct violation of the citation-traceability check: the record makes a specific factual claim about what a named source says/doesn't say, for a source that was never actually cited or shown to have been consulted.

records.name_note: The given name is already the currently accepted binomial (RHS lists "Name Status: Correct" for Cycas revoluta). Despite the common name and superficial resemblance, UF/IFAS confirms this species is a gymnosperm cycad, not a true (angiosperm) palm.
records.toxicity_detail: All parts of the plant contain the toxin cycasin, with the seeds having the highest concentration; pets are attracted to the plant, and pet poisoning symptoms include nosebleeds, bruising, and blood in stools (NC State). UF/IFAS independently states the plant "contains a powerful neurotoxin" and that seeds "can also be poisonous to humans and animals if ingested." RHS separately lists Cycas revoluta as "TOXIC to pets (dogs, cats)."
unknowns: chill_damage_f: sources give a survival floor (will not survive below 15°F per NC State and MOBOT) and vague frost damage occurring when temps 'briefly dip into the high teens' (MOBOT), not a precise damage-onset number, so left null.
day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives day- or night-specific temperature ranges for this species.
cool_rest_note: no source frames a temperature-based winter rest/dormancy requirement; RHS notes only reduced winter watering ('sparingly at other times'), not a temperature target.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: no admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule specific to Cycas revoluta. Clemson HGIC's palm-nutrient-deficiency note lives in a combined 'Palms & Cycads' factsheet and is not clearly attributed to cycads versus true palms, so it was not used.
humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: RHS gives only a qualitative 'moderate humidity' note; no source gives a percentage range.
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no source gives an indoor footcandle figure; only an outdoor sun-exposure category and an indoor filtered-light duration (4-6 hours) were found.

soil_base: sources describe amended potting mixes (loam-based compost with leaf mould and grit, or soil-based mix amended with sand and peat) rather than a single categorical soil_base type, so left null.
soil_ph_min: NC State lists this species under the 'Acid (<6.0)' pH category with no defined lower numeric bound given, so left null.

water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no source gives a watering-frequency interval in days or a probe-depth figure; only qualitative moisture guidance was found.

water_regime — removed on audit: water_regime='dry_surface_between' rests solely on MOBOT's prose ('Needs regular and consistent moisture with soil surface nearly drying between water applications'), but MOBOT's own structured Culture field for this exact page reads 'Water: Medium' -- not the drier 'Low' rating that a genuine dry-down regime would normally carry in that same rating system. NC State, cited elsewhere in this record for soil_drainage, independently describes the species as wanting soil that is 'moist and well-drained... intolerant to overwatering,' which reads as a request for consistent moisture rather than an explicit allow-to-dry cycle. This is exactly the case check #2 warns about: a harm-adjacent field (overwatering is called out by NC State as capable of causing root rot/plant death) where a cited source's own structured field sits in tension with the specific prose sentence quoted, and a second source's independent language doesn't clearly resolve it -- yet the record picked a specific value instead of softening or nulling it.

direct_sun_hours_max — removed on audit: The number 6 is lifted verbatim from NC State's 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' category -- confirmed present in NC State's actual page text. But outdoor_sun_exposure also includes full_sun, sourced independently from UF/IFAS ('grows well in full sun or partial shade') and MOBOT ('Full sun to part shade'), neither of which gives any hours figure, and NC State itself does not list this species under a 'Full Sun' category at all (only 'Partial Shade' appears in its structured Light field). Presenting 6 as the sun-hours ceiling while simultaneously endorsing full_sun as a valid outdoor exposure implies capping full-sun exposure at 6 hours/day, a claim none of the three sources actually make -- the number is scoped only to the narrower partial-shade band it was quoted from.

humidity_need — removed on audit: The only humidity statement anywhere in the RHS source ('moderate humidity', confirmed present verbatim) sits inside the single sentence 'Grow under glass in a peat-free, loam-based potting compost with additional leaf mould and grit; provide full light with shade from hot sun and moderate humidity' -- RHS's UK greenhouse/under-glass cultivation instructions for a plant not hardy outdoors there, not a general statement about the species' ambient humidity preference. The record generalized this glasshouse-specific clause into a blanket humidity_need value without flagging the narrower context, and no other admissible source (NC State, MOBOT, UF/IFAS) mentions humidity at all, so there is no independent corroboration for treating 'moderate/average' as the species' general requirement rather than an artifact of UK glasshouse culture advice.

water_dry_down_target — removed on audit: This field has no citation entry of its own in the citations array -- it silently reuses the same MOBOT quote already cited for water_regime, rather than being independently listed. Per structural check #1 ('does every non-null field value trace to at least one entry'), the trace here is only implicit through an identical underlying quote shared with another field, not an explicit, dedicated citation for this specific field.

chill_damage_f: no source gives a Fahrenheit damage-onset temperature. RHS gives only a categorical hardiness rating (H5: hardy in most UK locations even in severe winters, roughly -15 to -10°C) and Penn State/Missouri Botanical Garden describe zone-level winter-hardiness (USDA Zones 6-9) and bud-kill risk in general terms — these are survival/hardiness-zone statements, not a specific damage-onset figure, so were not mapped onto this field.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: sources give differing numeric pH thresholds tied to flower-color change rather than a stated survival/growth range, and they disagree with each other — Clemson HGIC and UMD Extension put the pink-flower threshold at pH 6.0 (Clemson) to 6.0-6.5 (UMD), while UGA Cooperative Extension puts it at pH 7.0 or higher; NC State and RHS give only broad Acid/Neutral/Alkaline categories with no numeric bound. humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source for this outdoor garden shrub.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good: not stated by any source — all give outdoor sun-exposure categories (full sun/part shade/dappled/deep shade), not indoor footcandle light levels; this species is not documented as grown under measured indoor light.

direct_sun_hours_max: sources give categorical light descriptions (e.g., NC State's 'Partial Shade' category is defined as 2-6 hours) but no source states a specific maximum sun-hours figure for this species itself.
fertilize_interval_days: Clemson HGIC gives specific calendar months (March, May, July) for fertilizing rather than a day-interval figure, so a numeric interval was not invented.

water_dormant_days_est, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm: no admissible source gives a winter/dormant-season watering frequency, a soil dry-down target, or a moisture-check depth for this deciduous shrub; Clemson's guidance is a fixed weekly landscape schedule, not a soil-moisture-check method.

cool_rest_note: no source frames this species' winter dormancy as a deliberate 'cool rest' care step; it is simply described as a deciduous shrub that drops its leaves and sets next year's flower buds on old wood over winter.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Verified NC State's actual page structure by fetching it directly: 'Poison Severity: Low', 'Poison Symptoms: nausea, stomach pain, vomiting, sweating', and 'Poison Toxic Principle: hydracyanosides (cyanogenic glycosides)' sit in one shared 'Poison Details' block, while 'Poisonous to Humans', 'Problem for Cats', 'Problem for Dogs', and 'Problem for Horses' are listed as parallel sibling tags in the same hazards list -- NOT nested inside a human-only 'Poisonous to Humans' section that structurally excludes pets. The record's toxicity_detail invents that humans-only/pets-excluded structure ('documented specifically under a Poisonous to Humans section... not for pets') to justify omitting the symptom/toxic-principle detail from the pet field, misrepresenting the source's actual layout -- this is exactly the 'structured fields contradict the prose used' failure mode. Separately, none of the specific facts stated in toxicity_detail's prose (severity rating, the four-symptom list, or the 'hydracyanosides/cyanogenic glycosides' toxic-principle name) appear in any `quote` field anywhere in the citations array, so this content does not trace to a citation entry as required.

water_regime — removed on audit: Two of the three citations backing 'keep_moist' are genus-level boilerplate, not species-specific evidence. Fetched Clemson's factsheet directly: the quoted sentence ('Maintain consistent moisture to prevent wilting and flower loss.') sits under a 'Watering Considerations for Hydrangeas' heading, and the same factsheet explicitly covers six hydrangea species/types (bigleaf, climbing, oakleaf, smooth, peegee, mountain) with the caveat 'Each hydrangea species thrives in slightly different growing conditions' -- this is not a bigleaf-only passage. The UGA CAES citation never names Hydrangea macrophylla anywhere in the article and uses 'hydrangeas' generically throughout, confirmed by direct fetch. Only the UMD citation is confirmed (via fetch) to sit specifically under a 'Bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla)' section heading -- the other two citations are reused genus-wide statements improperly presented as species-specific support.

water_growing_days_est — removed on audit: water_estimate_basis explicitly asserts the '7' figure is 'Based on Clemson Cooperative Extension's landscape watering guidance for in-ground bigleaf hydrangea,' but direct fetch of the Clemson page shows the sourced sentence ('Water deeply once per week, or more often during dry conditions.') sits inside a general 'Watering Considerations for Hydrangeas' section that the factsheet applies across all the hydrangea species/types it documents, not a bigleaf-specific passage. The field mischaracterizes generic once-per-week genus guidance as bigleaf-macrophylla-specific evidence.

outdoor_sun_exposure — removed on audit: The array includes 'full_sun' unconditionally alongside 'deep_shade', but direct fetch confirms NC State's species-specific structured Light field for Hydrangea macrophylla lists only 'Dappled Sunlight', 'Deep shade', and 'Partial Shade' -- Full Sun is not offered as an option at all for this species on that source. The record's own Missouri Botanical Garden citation only supports full sun conditionally ('Tolerates full sun only if grown in consistently moist soils'), a caveat that is dropped when 'full_sun' is added as an unqualified member of the flat exposure array. This is a case where a species-specific structured source (NC State) omits the value entirely and another source supports it only conditionally, yet the record encodes it as an unconditional option -- a plant-harm-relevant overstatement (full sun without consistent moisture risks scorch/wilt for this species).

records.toxicity_detail: UGA Cooperative Extension classifies Colchicum autumnale as "Major Toxicity, Dermatitis" on its pet-safety list: major toxicity means it "may result in serious illness or death if ingested," and dermatitis means "contact with thorns or sap may result in a skin rash." Missouri Botanical Garden notes the toxic alkaloid colchicine comes from the corms and seeds.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: no source gives a damage-onset cold threshold. NCSU/Missouri Botanical Garden give winter-survival hardiness figures instead ("hardy to about -4 degrees F"; dormant bulbs withstand soil temperatures "down to at least 23 degrees F"), which describe survival, not damage-onset, so this was not mapped to chill_damage_f.
day_f_min/day_f_max, night_f_min/night_f_max: no source gives day/night temperature ranges for this outdoor hardy bulb (USDA zones 4-8/9 per NCSU and Missouri Botanical Garden).
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any source.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: not addressed; the outdoor sources give a sun-duration category (full sun / partial shade) rather than an indoor footcandle figure.
direct_sun_hours_max: NCSU defines 'Full sun' as '6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day,' which is a minimum threshold defining the category, not a maximum cap, so it was not mapped to this field.
fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no source addresses fertilizing.

water_regime, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_estimate_basis, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est: Missouri Botanical Garden describes a seasonal cycle ('Reduce watering when the foliage yellows and begins to die back (July). Resume watering again in late summer') and RHS notes it is 'Intolerant of waterlogging,' but neither maps cleanly onto one of the fixed water_regime categories or gives a numeric interval/depth, so these were left null rather than forced.

cool_rest_note: the dormancy described by Missouri Botanical Garden is a summer dry-dormancy tied to foliage die-back (not a cool/winter rest), so this field was left null rather than mismatched to a winter-rest framing.

is_houseplant: no source describes growing this species indoors or in containers long-term; NCSU lists 'Container' only as one of several outdoor Landscape Location categories alongside Lawn/Meadow/Woodland, and RHS's suggested planting locations are all outdoor garden settings, so is_houseplant was set to false.

PSU Extension ('The Unexpected Delight of Fall-Blooming Bulbs') discusses 'Colchicum species' generically -- including a statement that 'All parts of the colchicum plant are poisonous to humans and animals' -- but never names the binomial Colchicum autumnale on that page, so per the genus-vs-species rule it was excluded as a citation here even though its content is consistent with the NCSU/RHS/UGA species-specific sources used.

name_note — removed on audit: The parenthetical calling Crocus sativus 'a different genus, family Iridaceae, and non-toxic' has no supporting citation for the 'non-toxic' claim anywhere in the array — none of the cited quotes make any toxicity statement about Crocus sativus. This smuggles an unsourced toxicity assertion about a different genus into a field that's supposed to be scoped to Colchicum autumnale naming/confusion, and it's exactly the kind of claim that needs an admissible-source citation given the record's own emphasis on toxicity accuracy.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: is_houseplant:false leans on citation 17's NC State quote 'Landscape Location: Container Lawn Meadow Woodland,' with the claim label asserting 'landscape placements are all outdoor' — but 'Container' is not inherently an outdoor category (container/patio growing commonly includes indoor use) and the quote never states outdoor-only. The false value is derived from the absence of an explicit 'Houseplant' tag rather than any source affirmatively saying this species isn't grown indoors, which is an inference from silence rather than a sourced fact.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: restored after the first audit pass nulled the field over a defect in one of three supporting citations (NC State's claim label over-asserted "dogs" when its quote only names cats). The audit's own reasoning confirmed the true/false direction is independently supported by RHS ("TOXIC to pets") and UGA (species-named "Major Toxicity, Dermatitis"); toxicity_detail is rebuilt from those two citations' quotes only, dropping the unsupported dogs/horses claim and the "toxic alkaloid" editorial gloss the audit flagged on citation 10.

records.name_note: NC State Extension and Missouri Botanical Garden both maintain dedicated profiles under the binomial "Rheum rhabarbarum" (MOBOT's page for the popular 'Victoria' cultivar is filed under that name, with its own species-level culture notes), so scientific_name_accepted is kept identical to the given name. However, the Royal Horticultural Society instead calls cultivated garden rhubarb "Rheum × hybridum" throughout its growing guides ("Rhubarb (Rheum × hybridum) is a hardy perennial... Botanical name: Rheum x hybridum") and never uses "rhabarbarum." None of the three admissible sources explicitly states that one name is a synonym of, or supersedes, the other, so no switch to Rheum × hybridum was made here. Readers should be aware that garden/culinary rhubarb is sometimes classified under that separate hybrid name by other authorities.
records.cool_rest_note: Hardy; needs no winter protection, and exposure to cold is necessary to trigger new growth in spring (per RHS overwintering guidance).
unknowns: day_f_max/day_f_min/night_f_max/night_f_min: no admissible source gives numeric day/night temperature thresholds; the UF/IFAS EDIS publication most relevant to cultivation temperature (HS657/MV124, 'Rhubarb') returns '410 Gone' on the admissible ask.ifas.ufl.edu domain ('This Publication is no longer supported on AskIFAS'), so its figures could not be used, and no other admissible source gives numbers.

chill_damage_f: RHS only warns qualitatively that late frosts can damage young stems ('best not to plant it in a site prone to late frosts, as the young stems may be damaged'); no source gives a specific damage-onset temperature.

water_regime: left null due to a genuine conflict - Missouri Botanical Garden's Rheum rhabarbarum 'Victoria' page says established plants need 'regular, consistently even moisture,' while RHS says established plants need watering 'only during prolonged dry periods in summer' and otherwise rarely need water. These outdoor garden-watering descriptions also don't map cleanly onto the keep_moist/dry_surface_between/dry_thoroughly_between/keep_barely_moist container-care framework.

soil_drainage: left null - Missouri Botanical Garden describes the soil as 'medium moisture, well-drained soils' while RHS calls for 'moisture-retentive soil that doesn't get waterlogged'; these phrasings pull toward different ends of a fast/moderate/moisture_retentive scale and neither source resolves the tension, so no single enum value was asserted.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: Missouri Botanical Garden describes the preferred soil only qualitatively as 'slightly acidic'; no admissible source gives a numeric pH range.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: RHS gives only a one-time application rate ('a general fertiliser such as Growmore in spring or summer at 70g per sq m') and general mulch-for-nutrients advice, not a repeat interval, specific calendar months, or a dose-strength (full/half/quarter) framework.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity; all describe outdoor garden-bed or outdoor large-container cultivation.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: all admissible sources describe light only via the outdoor sun/shade duration category (full sun / part shade / light shade), not footcandle values or an hours-of-direct-sun figure.

water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no source gives a soil-check depth, a dry-down description, or day-interval watering estimates; these are container-houseplant-style metrics not used by the outdoor garden sources found for this species.

is_houseplant: only NC State Extension's 'Found in' tag ('Houseplant or interiorscape') supports indoor/container use; RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden describe only outdoor garden-bed or outdoor large-container culture and do not address indoor houseplant growing.

scientific_name_accepted: NC State Extension and Missouri Botanical Garden both use 'Rheum rhabarbarum' as a standing name with their own dedicated records, while RHS uses 'Rheum × hybridum' for the same cultivated garden plant and never uses 'rhabarbarum'; no source states one is a synonym of the other, so the given name was kept rather than asserting a change (see name_note).

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Two problems verified against the live NC State page (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rheum-rhabarbarum/). (1) The closing sentence 'Does not cause contact dermatitis' is real content on the source (a 'Causes Contact Dermatitis: No' field) but is not present in any of the citation quotes (citations 3-6 never mention dermatitis) -- it fails structural check #1 that every non-null field value trace to a citation entry; it was smuggled into the field from the source without being logged as a citation. (2) The bulk of the symptom list used -- 'abdominal cramps, burning of the mouth and throat, headache, weakness, nausea and vomiting, and possibly fatal coma' -- comes verbatim from NC State's Human Toxicity section (confirmed live: the page groups this text under 'Human Toxicity Severity: Medium severity poison characteristics'), not from pet-specific data. Only the trailing clause ('Kidney failure (in grazing animals), salivation in dogs/cats') is animal-specific. toxicity_detail presents the whole block as one undifferentiated toxicity narrative supporting toxic_to_pets=true, which risks implying pets show symptoms like 'headache' and 'weakness' that are documented only for human poisoning victims -- exactly the human/animal conflation the audit's check #3 warns against.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: The only support is a single NC State 'Found In' tag ('Houseplant or interiorscape'), which conflicts with the rest of the same record: cool_rest_note (from RHS) states rhubarb needs 'exposure to cold... to trigger new growth in spring' and 'needs no protection over winter'; RHS separately calls it a hardy perennial that 'thrives in even the coldest sites'; MOBOT gives it USDA zones 3-8 and a 2-5 ft outdoor spread. soil_base is asserted only as garden_bed, with no container/indoor pairing. Neither of the other two admissible sources (RHS, MOBOT) mentions indoor or houseplant culture at all. A cold-dormancy-requiring, multi-foot perennial with documented leaf/root toxicity is not a plausible houseplant, and the record never reconciles this internal contradiction before asserting true.

outdoor_sun_exposure: restored to full_sun/part_shade using Missouri Botanical Garden's citation alone ("full sun to part shade," an exact match to both enum values). The first pass had paired this with an RHS citation whose quote says "light shade," not "part shade" -- that citation's claim label was narrowed to the soil-moisture point it actually supports rather than re-asserting a sun-exposure claim its quote doesn't make.

records.name_note: Buxus sempervirens is the currently accepted binomial for common/European boxwood; RHS lists its Name Status as "Correct" (not a synonym). No source used here treats the given name as outdated.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: no cited source states a specific damage-onset temperature in °F; only USDA hardiness zones (5-8, per NC State/MOBOT/Clemson) and RHS's H6 survival hardiness rating (-20 to -15°C) are given, and those describe survival thresholds, not the temperature at which damage begins.
day_f_max, day_f_min, night_f_max, night_f_min: none of the cited outdoor/landscape sources give specific day or night temperature targets; cold tolerance is expressed only via USDA hardiness zone.
direct_sun_hours_max, light_fc_min, light_fc_good: sources give only categorical outdoor sun exposure (full sun/part shade/full shade), not a maximum-sun-hours figure or footcandle values.
fertilize_active_months: Clemson's general Boxwood cultivation guidance says to fertilize 'in the early spring' but names no specific months.
fertilize_interval_days: Clemson states boxwood 'do not need to be fertilized on an annual basis' and should be fertilized only after a soil test shows a need, so no fixed interval is given.
fertilize_strength: no cited source states a fertilizer strength or dilution rate.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no cited source discusses ambient humidity requirements for this outdoor landscape shrub.
cool_rest_note: no cited source describes a winter dormancy/rest period requirement.
water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target: no cited source gives a soil-check depth or a specific dry-down target between waterings.
water_dormant_days_est: Clemson only advises watering 'before extreme cold spells' in winter -- an event-driven cue, not a day-interval estimate.

soil_base: set to garden_bed based on in-ground/border landscape descriptions (MOBOT, Clemson). Note that RHS ('Patio and container plants'), Clemson ('used in containers'), NC State ('Landscape Location: Container'), and MOBOT ('large containers') all also describe boxwood grown in outdoor containers, but no source describes long-term indoor growing, and the schema has no distinct outdoor-container option.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The field states a specific toxic principle and symptom list ('steroidal alkaloids'; 'nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, convulsions, respiratory failure'; toxic part 'leaves') attributed to a 'Poisonous to Humans' section of the NC State page. None of the 15 entries in `citations` contains this quote or anything resembling it -- there is no source entry backing this specific content at all. Regardless of the field's own disclaimer that this data isn't being reused to support the pets conclusion, the content's mere presence in a non-null field with zero citation trace violates the basic citations-must-support-every-field-value rule.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The NC State citation's parenthetical gloss reads '(good drainage, tolerates occasional wetness)', but its quote is just the categorical tag 'Good Drainage' -- nothing about wetness tolerance. Worse, this directly contradicts the very next citation (Clemson) used for the same field: 'Never plant boxwood near downspouts or in any area that stays wet. They require well-drained soil.' One citation's added interpretive text says the plant tolerates occasional wetness while the paired citation for the same field says the opposite; the record didn't surface or resolve this contradiction, just merged both into 'moderate.'

soil_base — removed on audit: The record commits to a definitive 'garden_bed' value from a single MOBOT in-ground/loam description, yet its own unknowns note admits RHS ('Patio and container plants'), Clemson ('used in containers'), NC State ('Landscape Location: Container'), and MOBOT ('large containers') all also document container cultivation for this species. That's a genuinely disclosed source disagreement about primary growing context that got resolved by picking one value instead of leaving the field null or otherwise flagging the mixed evidence.

is_houseplant — removed on audit: No entry in `citations` supports this field at all -- there is no quote or source addressing indoor vs. outdoor cultivation status. While the value (false) is plausible given the outdoor-shrub context of every other field, it fails the basic requirement that every non-null field trace to a citation.

normalizations: 2026-08-22: first batch of the post-curated-catalog "blind spots" pass -- 8 species chosen by direct inspection of coverage gaps (no true lilies, azalea/rhododendron, oleander, sago palm, or hydrangea were in the catalog; rhubarb, boxwood and colchicum were also absent), prioritizing the single largest safety gap: no pet-toxic ornamentals beyond the food-crop cases already covered.

The batch's own post-audit cleanup nulls a field wholesale whenever any finding on it is refuted, even when the auditor's own reasoning says the value is independently supported by other, unflagged citations and only one supporting citation among several had a narrower defect. This wrongly zeroed out toxic_to_pets for Colchicum autumnale (Autumn Crocus) -- one of the more dangerous plants in this batch -- over a single citation's mislabeled "Problem for Dogs" claim, while its RHS "TOXIC to pets" and UGA "Major Toxicity, Dermatitis" citations (species-named, unflagged) went untouched. Restored directly at landing using only those two clean citations, not new research. The same pattern nulled Rhubarb's outdoor_sun_exposure over one mislabeled RHS citation while Missouri Botanical Garden's clean, unambiguous "full sun to part shade" citation was left standing unused -- also restored at landing. Future batch scripts should have the verify pass check remaining support before nulling, or refute per-citation rather than per-field.

Azalea (Rhododendron simsii) needed a second, targeted research pass: the first pass's only toxicity citation was a truncated, boilerplate-flavored RHS pet-safety tag with no species-specific content, and no citation established the accepted binomial at all. The retry found solid independent corroboration for toxicity (UGA and UF/IFAS, both naming azalea/Rhododendron spp. with a documented grayanotoxin mechanism), but on the naming question it surfaced a genuine, unresolved conflict rather than closing the gap: two distinct historical "Azalea indica" epithets (Linnaeus 1753 vs. Sims 1817) resolve to two different modern binomials (Rhododendron indicum vs. R. simsii), and RHS and NC State each independently anchor to a different one. scientific_name_accepted stays null on this species pending a source that resolves the conflict -- the right outcome per this catalog's own rule of refusing rather than picking a side on a genuine disagreement, now correctly reached for a naming question rather than only for a numeric one.

Sago Palm's own citations establish it is a cycad, not a true palm (UF/IFAS: "unrelated to true palms, which are actually angiosperms") -- confirmed no citation in this batch conflates its toxicity data with the unrelated palm genus already in the catalog (Chamaedorea/Chrysalidocarpus).
